brief: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO. JPMorgan's Michael Cembalest argues the scandal distracts from a bigger problem: Nvidia's chip and political position eroding. Of roughly 44GW in compute deals the frontier labs have announced for 2026 onward, Nvidia GPUs take only 28%, versus an 80-90% AI chip revenue share in 2024-2025, as labs diversify to Broadcom, AMD, Amazon and Google chips. The CUDA software moat is closing too: a frontier lab's onboarding time on AMD GPUs fell from 6-12 months to 3 days using AI-assisted engineering, and AMD's MI455X now benchmarks ahead of Nvidia's own Vera Rubin VR200. Simultaneously, Nvidia's other core market, Chinese open-weight compute, faces a new Commerce rule closing the "cloud loophole" on remote access to US chips, projected at 32% of China's AI compute by end-2027 and concentrated in Southeast Asia. This follows Nvidia's own lobbying history against export controls and undisclosed Singapore billing. Cembalest still calls the stock interesting for long-term holders at a 0.2x PEG, the cheapest large AI name, but says the competitive shift is as notable a risk as the leadership change.
